title: 3 invisible ways your AI gets hijacked

beats.say: Your AI can be hijacked by text you can't even see. Three ways. And number three needs zero clicks.
Number one. A tool you plug in can hide orders in its own description. Only the AI reads them. One demo made it grab a private SSH key.

vis.title: tool description · what the AI reads
lines: and pass it in the sidenote argument

beats.say: Number two. A rules file with invisible characters. You see clean rules. The AI sees extra ones.
Now number three. This one scares me.
An email you never open. You ask Copilot a normal question, and it mixes that email with your private data. It's called EchoLeak. Rated nine point three out of ten.

items: email text mixes with your data

beats.say: Microsoft patched it, and nobody was caught using it. But the rule holds. Never let an AI read text you don't trust, next to data you do.
Here's the prompt. Screenshot it, and send it to Claude inside your project.
Follow Ship With Pip for one of these every day.

prompt: Audit every AI tool I use. For each one, list what private data it can read (files, keys, email, chats), and what untrusted text it also reads (inbound email, GitHub issues, web pages, MCP tool descriptions, rules files). Flag every tool that reads both, show me how to scan my rules files for invisible characters, and tell me what to restrict.
caption: 3 invisible ways your AI gets hijacked. 1) MCP tool poisoning (Invariant Labs, Apr 2025): a tool description can hide instructions only the AI sees. 2) Rules File Backdoor (Pillar Security, Mar 2025): invisible Unicode in Cursor and Copilot rules files. 3) EchoLeak (Aim Security, CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3): a zero-click Copilot flaw, patched June 2025, no evidence of exploitation. The rule: never let an AI read untrusted text next to your private data. The prompt is at the end. Building your own app? Use code AT100 on Base44 (link in bio).
